<reason>A won by converting B's own concession ("forever was never literal") into the motion's premise: B ended up defending delay, not permanence, while the core arithmetic — recurring deaths on fixed acres, with London/Singapore/NY already at the wall — was never squarely answered, only met with asserted "smarter design." A also took the environmental clash ("sewage has a treatment plant; land scarcity has none") and answered both pressure questions directly with concrete mechanisms (named groves/columbaria, treatment capacity, untouched religious cemeteries). B's best ground — that abolition prices religious obligation and landless visiting out of public ground — survived only partially answered, and B's fix (exempt permanent sections) reintroduced the two-tier permanence scarcity forbids, which A exploited. B matched A rhetorically ("Mourners end too") and the tower-renter point was genuinely strong, but B never resolved why continued allocation works in a truly land-scarce city. A's clipped first rebuttal was a modest execution cost, not a substantive loss.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 1 move that "reuse after long rest" is "a confession that forever is already finished" — it reframed B's counter-model as evidence for the motion and set the terms for every later round; B's strongest counter ("those decades are the entire moral work of a grave") was rhetorically fine but conceded the permanence point the motion attacks.</best_rebuttal>
